name: Cognitive dissonance
statement: Acting against one's own beliefs is said to create a discomfort that people relieve by revising the belief rather than the act.
meaning: Festinger's claim is about pressure rather than logic. Two thoughts that do not sit together produce a drive state, and the drive pushes on whichever of them is easier to move. A deed already done cannot be moved, so the belief moves. The prediction that made the theory famous is the one about incentives, and it runs backwards from common sense. A large payment for saying something one does not believe supplies a reason for saying it, so little dissonance arises and the attitude stays put. A small payment leaves the act unexplained, and the attitude shifts to explain it. Less money, more persuasion.

origin.where: the book A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance
origin.note: The book set out the theory and named it. The experiment usually cited as its demonstration came two years later, in Festinger and Carlsmith's 1959 paper on forced compliance. The theory's other workhorse design predates the book: Brehm's 1956 free-choice study of post-decision changes in desirability.

evidence: Seventy-one male students spent an hour turning pegs and stacking spools, a task built to be dull. Each was then asked to tell the next participant, waiting outside, that the work had been interesting, and was paid either one dollar or twenty dollars to say it. A control group told nobody anything. Eleven participants were dropped for reasons including suspicion about the payment, leaving twenty per condition. Asked afterwards how enjoyable the tasks had been, on a scale running from -5 to +5, the control group averaged -0.45 and the twenty-dollar group -0.05. The one-dollar group averaged +1.35, differing from the control at t = 2.48, p = .02, and from the twenty-dollar group at t = 2.22, p = .03.

replication.headline: A 39-lab preregistered replication of the induced-compliance experiment found nothing, while a corrected version of the free-choice experiment still finds a small effect.
replication.detail: Vaidis and colleagues ran induced compliance in 39 laboratories across 19 countries, following Croyle and Cooper's 1983 Experiment 1 rather than the peg-turning study. Participants wrote an essay against their own view under high or low choice. A pretest across the labs picked an increase in tuition fees as the default topic, and labs for which it did not fit could substitute another. The manipulation worked: high-choice participants felt freer to refuse, d = 0.77, 95% CI [0.69, 0.84]. Their attitudes did not follow. Across 38 labs and 3,822 participants the high-choice group ended at 2.60 and the low-choice group at 2.66, d = -0.03, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.04]. The same authors put the Croyle and Cooper original at d = 2.40, 95% CI [1.40, 3.37]. Writing the essay at all moved attitudes relative to writing a neutral one, d = 0.26, 95% CI [0.18, 0.34], which is advocacy working without the choice the theory requires. The other paradigm has its own history. In the free-choice design people rate two items, choose between them, then rate again. Chen and Risen proved that this shows the alternatives spreading apart even when no preference has changed, because the choice reveals preference that the ratings measured imprecisely. Corrected designs followed. Izuma and Murayama pooled four of them at d = 0.26, 95% CI [0.10, 0.42], and advised abandoning the uncorrected version. Enisman, Shpitzer and Kleiman later pooled 43 artifact-free studies, N = 2,191, at d = 0.40, 95% CI [0.32, 0.49], and found no sign of publication bias.

study.cite: Vaidis, D. C., Sleegers, W. W. A., van Leeuwen, F., DeMarree, K. G., Sætrevik, B., Ross, R. M., et al. (2024). A multilab replication of the induced-compliance paradigm of cognitive dissonance. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 7(1).

limits: The verdict on this page is one word covering two paradigms that have different evidence behind them. The effect sizes recorded in the structured fields, 2.40 against -0.03, belong to induced compliance alone. The free-choice figures sit in the prose above and are not comparable with them: they come from meta-analyses of corrected designs, not from a single replication of a single study. A reader who takes the headline number as the state of dissonance research has taken half of it. The multilab study replicates a descendant of the 1959 experiment rather than the experiment. No large preregistered attempt at the peg-turning design was located in this search, which covered Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC and web search. The d = 2.40 figure is Vaidis and colleagues' estimate of the 1983 result, not a number the 1983 paper printed. Nuttin published a critical replication of Festinger and Carlsmith in 1966, in the International Journal of Psychology; the text is paywalled, it was not read for this entry, and nothing is claimed about what it found. Cyrus-Lai, Tierney and Uhlmann published a commentary in the same journal as the multilab study, asking what one can conclude when a classic finding fails to replicate, and that argument was likewise not read here. Dissonance theory reaches beyond these two paradigms, to effort justification and hypocrisy induction among others, and those literatures were not searched.
misreadings: The 1959 study is retold as proof that paying people less makes them believe more. That held for twenty men in one room, and no large replication of it has been located. The 39-lab null is then read the opposite way, as proof that dissonance does not exist. What it shows is that one procedure does not reliably produce attitude change, which its authors state as choice being either unnecessary or necessary but insufficient. The free-choice literature carries the sharper lesson. For half a century a design measured the alternatives spreading apart, and the spreading was read as preference change. Chen and Risen's central point is a theorem rather than a finding: the design returns spreading even when preferences are fixed. What survived the correction is much smaller than what was claimed, and it did survive.

sources.text: Festinger, L. (1957). A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance. Stanford University Press. The book that named the theory.

Festinger, L., & Carlsmith, J. M. (1959). Cognitive consequences of forced compliance. The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 58(2), 203-210. Source for every number in the evidence section, read from the full text.
Brehm, J. W. (1956). Postdecision changes in the desirability of alternatives. The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 52(3), 384-389. The first free-choice experiment.

Croyle, R. T., & Cooper, J. (1983). Dissonance arousal: Physiological evidence. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 45(4), 782-791. Experiment 1 is the study the multilab replication followed.

Vaidis, D. C., Sleegers, W. W. A., van Leeuwen, F., DeMarree, K. G., Sætrevik, B., Ross, R. M., et al. (2024). A multilab replication of the induced-compliance paradigm of cognitive dissonance. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 7(1).

Chen, M. K., & Risen, J. L. (2010). How choice affects and reflects preferences: Revisiting the free-choice paradigm. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 99(4), 573-594. The argument that the paradigm measures spreading without preference change.
Izuma, K., & Murayama, K. (2013). Choice-induced preference change in the free-choice paradigm: A critical methodological review. Frontiers in Psychology, 4, 41.

Enisman, M., Shpitzer, H., & Kleiman, T. (2021). Choice changes preferences, not merely reflects them: A meta-analysis of the artifact-free free-choice paradigm. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 120(1), 16-29.

Nuttin, J. M. (1966). Attitude change after rewarded dissonant and consonant forced compliance: A critical replication of the Festinger and Carlsmith experiment. International Journal of Psychology, 1(1), 39-57. Listed because it exists; the text was not read for this entry.

Cyrus-Lai, W., Tierney, W., & Uhlmann, E. L. (2024). Noise versus signal: What can one conclude when a classic finding fails to replicate? Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 7(4). Commentary; the text was not read for this entry.
